title: The Vendor Finance Trap: Why Being Paid Over Time Means You Haven't Fully Sold Your Business
excerpt: Vendor finance can bridge a valuation gap and close a stalled sale, but once settlement happens, the risk of the business performing well enough to repay it belongs to someone else.
content:
You agree a sale price for the business, and on paper it is close to the number you had been hoping for. Then the fine print lands: a portion of that price will not be paid at settlement. It is structured as vendor finance, a seller note the buyer repays over the next one to three years out of the earnings the business generates once it is no longer yours to run.

The headline figure does not move. What changes, quietly, is who carries the risk of the business performing well enough to actually pay it. Settlement day feels like the finish line. For the deferred portion of the deal, it is closer to the starting line of a different kind of exposure, one you no longer have the authority to manage.

What vendor finance is, and why buyers ask for it

Vendor finance, sometimes called a seller note, is a loan the seller extends to the buyer as part of the purchase price, repaid with interest over an agreed term rather than paid in full on settlement day. It turns up in Australian SME sales for a few recurring reasons. The buyer cannot secure the full price from a bank on workable terms. There is a gap between what the seller believes the business is worth and what a lender will fund against it. Or the buyer, reasonably enough, wants the seller's confidence in the handover reflected in the terms, not just in the conversation that led up to signing.

It shows up most often in owner-operated businesses changing hands to management, family, or a buyer without deep capital behind them, the kind of sale where relationships and know-how genuinely matter to whether performance holds up after handover.

Where the exposure actually sits once you no longer run the place

The pattern we typically see across owner-led sales is that owners negotiate price hard and walk past structure. Once settlement happens, every decision that determines whether the business can service that note now belongs to someone else. Pricing calls, staffing decisions, how tightly debtors are managed, whether the new owner takes on fresh debt or capital spending, all of it sits with them, not with you. A soft quarter, a key staff departure, or a new owner running working capital looser than you did can all show up as a late or renegotiated repayment, and from outside the business, there is very little practical leverage to intervene.

Vendor finance is also usually subordinated, meaning if the business runs into genuine difficulty, the bank and other secured creditors are repaid first. The note that looked like part of your sale price can end up ranking behind debt the new owner takes on after you have already left the building, a risk that a thorough exit readiness process is built to price in before terms are agreed, not discover afterward.

How to structure the protection before you sign, not after

Vendor finance is not inherently a weak structure. It can bridge a genuine valuation gap and keep a deal alive that would otherwise stall at the financing stage. The difference between a note that works and one that quietly erodes your sale price is whether you treat the buyer as a borrower during negotiation, not simply as a counterparty you are relieved to have found.

That means security over business assets registered on the PPSR, not just a signature on a loan agreement. It means consent rights over the decisions most likely to affect repayment, such as taking on further debt, selling key assets, or a change of control before the note is cleared. It means a term short enough that your exposure does not stretch across several trading cycles, and triggers that bring repayment forward if agreed conditions, like minimum revenue or an existing facility, are breached. None of this is unusual to ask for. It is the same diligence a bank would run on the buyer, applied by the party actually extending the credit.

An independent business valuation done ahead of negotiation gives you the standing to ask for these terms from a position of clarity, rather than relief that an offer has finally arrived. The number itself matters less than understanding which parts of it you are genuinely prepared to carry risk on, and for how long.

The sale price is the number everyone discusses. The structure behind it decides how much of that number you actually keep, and when. If a deal on the table includes a vendor finance component, it is worth working through the terms with the same rigour you would bring to any other lending decision, before you sign rather than after. An exit readiness diagnostic is built for exactly this kind of structural question. If you want a second set of eyes on where a vendor finance arrangement leaves you exposed, book a discovery call and bring the term sheet with you.

faqs.q: What is vendor finance when selling a business in Australia?
faqs.a: Vendor finance, also called a seller note, is when the person selling a business lends part of the purchase price back to the buyer, who repays it with interest over an agreed term instead of receiving everything at settlement. It is common in owner-operated Australian SME sales where the buyer cannot fund the full price through a bank alone. Our exit readiness guide covers how this fits into a wider sale structure.

faqs.q: How much of a business sale price is usually structured as vendor finance?
faqs.a: There is no fixed proportion. It depends on the buyer's financing capacity, how much a lender is prepared to fund against the business, and how much confidence the seller is willing to show in the handover. What matters more than the percentage is whether the deferred portion is properly secured and time limited, rather than left as an informal arrangement between two parties who trust each other on the day of signing.

faqs.q: Can a seller take security over the business after offering vendor finance?
faqs.a: Yes. A seller extending vendor finance can register a security interest over business assets on the Personal Property Securities Register, in the same way a bank would. This gives the seller a formal claim if repayments stop, rather than relying on goodwill. An exit readiness diagnostic is a useful place to work through what security is realistic to ask for before terms are finalised.

faqs.q: What happens if a buyer stops repaying a vendor finance note?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on how the note was structured. Without security or consent rights, a seller's options are limited and often expensive, usually legal action against a business they no longer control. With a registered security interest, acceleration triggers and clear covenants in place, a seller has a genuine enforcement path rather than a difficult conversation with no leverage behind it.

faqs.q: Is vendor finance common in small business sales across Queensland and NSW?
faqs.a: It turns up regularly in owner-operated sales across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, particularly where the buyer is existing management, a family member, or a smaller operator without institutional backing. It is less common in larger transactions involving private equity or trade buyers with full access to acquisition finance already arranged.

faqs.q: Does offering vendor finance change how a business should be valued before sale?
faqs.a: It does not change the underlying value of the business, but it changes how much of that value you actually receive, and when. A business valuation done before negotiation gives you a clear independent number to negotiate structure against, rather than letting the buyer's financing constraints quietly set both the price and the terms of the sale.

faqs.q: Should a seller get advice before agreeing to vendor finance terms?
faqs.a: Yes, because the terms function as a lending decision, not just a sale clause. Treating the buyer the way a bank would, with proper security, covenants and a defined term, protects the portion of your sale price you have not yet been paid. A discovery call is a good place to start working through the specific terms of an offer.
